title: USDA to Airdrop Rabies Vaccines for Wildlife Across Southeast
summary:
Next month, planes will fly over parts of the Southeastern United States, dropping millions of small, fishmeal-coated packets into the wilderness. These aren't treats — they're oral rabies vaccine baits, part of a massive effort to stop the spread of a deadly disease.

Rabies is one of the oldest known diseases, and it's almost always fatal once symptoms appear. It kills around 59,000 people worldwide each year. In the U.S., about 90 percent of cases occur in wildlife like raccoons, skunks, bats, and foxes. Since 1995, the USDA's National Rabies Management Program has been working to control the disease by distributing these vaccine baits.

The operation is huge. Millions of baits are dropped across thousands of square miles in Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Georgia, and Alabama. The goal, according to a USDA spokesperson, is to "prevent westward spread of raccoon rabies by creating a continuous vaccine barrier that stays in front of rabies occurrence on the landscape."

The baits are specifically designed to target the rabies variants found in raccoons, coyotes, and gray foxes. They're coated in fishmeal to attract animals. The vaccine inside is proven safe for over 60 species, including cats and dogs. If you find one in a residential area, the USDA recommends leaving it alone or using gloves to move it to a more remote location. Always wash your hands afterward — and try to ignore the pungent fishy odor.

The program has been so successful that the USDA is close to establishing an ORV area in South Carolina counties bordering North Carolina and Georgia in the next few years. If all goes as planned, the geographic scope of the program will shrink over time as rabies is eliminated regionally. Combating rabies costs the U.S. over $300 million annually, but the price is justified by the lives saved — both animal and human.
why_it_matters: Rabies control shows how public health works at the meeting point of humans, animals and the environment: a vaccine dropped in a forest can prevent a deadly human infection years later, and the cost-benefit math behind such programs is the kind of hard choice governments make about prevention every day.

background_read: Rabies is an ancient viral disease that attacks the brain and nerves. Once symptoms appear it is almost always fatal, but it can be prevented by vaccination given soon after a bite or scratch.

Worldwide, most human deaths come from dog bites, and the World Health Organization (the United Nations agency that coordinates global public health) counts tens of thousands of deaths a year, mostly in Asia and Africa.

In the United States, dog rabies was largely eliminated during the 20th century through pet vaccination laws, which shifted the danger to wildlife — especially the raccoon variant of the virus that spread up the East Coast in the 1970s and 1980s.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (the government department responsible for farming, food and forests, which also handles wildlife disease) began large-scale bait drops in 1995. A similar campaign in Texas is credited with wiping out the coyote form of rabies there, and European countries used plane-dropped baits to all but eliminate fox rabies across much of Western Europe.
These campaigns follow the same pattern as other successful disease-eradication efforts: consistent funding, years of monitoring, and a clear geographic goal.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — public health and pet owners
perspectives.description: The bait drops have held raccoon rabies back from spreading west and have protected pets, livestock and people. The vaccine is proven safe for over 60 species, and the program costs far less than treating human rabies cases.

Some people are uneasy about government planes scattering vaccine-laden packets near homes, wondering what happens if a child or pet picks one up. Others question whether taxpayer money should fund wildlife medicine, especially in states where human rabies cases are already very rare.

This is a textbook example of a wildlife disease eradication campaign, like the effort that removed fox rabies from much of Western Europe. Such programs take decades of steady funding and surveillance, and because bats carry their own rabies variants, total elimination of the disease is not realistic.

Officials expect to add an ORV zone in South Carolina counties, and if the plan works the program's footprint could steadily shrink as regions are declared rabies-free. That success would raise a new challenge: keeping surveillance and funding strong once the danger feels distant.
